summary: Turnrow is a free web app designed for farmers. Its purpose is to help them better understand their field’s conditions and, based on this information, choose the crop rotation that fits them best. The farmer enters some information about their field, their crops, and their priorities. Turnrow then uses 25 years of NASA POWER weather data, together with soil and slope data for the farmer’s location, to test 32 crops against those 25 years. It compares the farmer’s current rotation with the alternatives it finds and highlights the gains and costs of changing. This matters because many farmers are older and less used to complicated digital tools. Turnrow gives them a chance to use data they normally could not, through a simple dashboard with numbered steps, in seven languages, so they can improve their fields in the way they choose.
details:
What it does and how it works. Turnrow is a free web app that helps farmers understand their field and choose a crop rotation that fits it. The farmer taps their field on a map. Turnrow loads 25 years of daily NASA weather for that exact spot, the slope of the land, and satellite layers showing crop greenness, soil wetness and rainfall. The farmer lists the crops they grow and picks what matters most: saving water, soil health, income or stopping erosion. Turnrow then tests each crop against that field’s own weather record (frost, heat, rain and soil water) and compares the farmer’s current rotation with at least two alternatives. Each option explains why it was suggested, the evidence behind it, what the farmer gains, what it costs, and what to check locally, as numbered steps and a month-by-month calendar.

Benefits and impact. Weather is becoming harder to predict and the old planting rules no longer hold. Many farmers are older and less used to complicated digital tools, so NASA’s open data rarely reaches them. Turnrow gives them a plan they can act on instead of a dashboard. It is free, needs no login, works on a phone and comes in seven languages. Our aim is to help farmers protect their soil, water and income. Turnrow supports a farmer’s judgment; it does not replace it.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the map and Netlify for hosting. No special hardware is needed: it runs in any browser. Data comes live from NASA POWER, NASA GIBS satellite layers (SMAP, GPM, MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat, GRACE) and SRTM terrain, with ERA5, the USDA soil survey and FAO crop tables as partner data. We used an AI assistant for coding, translation and the logo, and this is disclosed in the app.

Creativity. The farmer’s own priorities change the ranking, so two farmers on the same land can get different advice. Sliders let the farmer test every result under a hotter or drier future. Everything is reduced to simple steps and three colours: green is good, yellow is watch, red is risk.

What we considered. Simplicity for people with no technical background; honesty, so every option shows what the tool does not know; and realism, so it suggests trying a change on part of the field first. We tried it on example fields in Portugal, the United States, India and Kenya, and the app compares NASA rainfall with a second, independent record. Its limits: crop values are general averages, soil data is detailed only for the US, and it has not yet been tested with farmers in the field.
dataRefs: NASA POWER – daily weather data since 2001
NASA SRTM – terrain height and slope
NASA MODIS – vegetation greenness and land temperature
projectRefs: ESA Sentinel-2 MSI – detailed vegetation imagery (data via NASA Earthdata)
USDA Soil Data Access (SSURGO soil survey)
FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 – crop water requirements
Terrain Tiles on AWS – elevation data
OpenStreetMap – base map and place search
Claude (Anthropic) – AI assistant used for coding and translation
FAO ECOCROP – crop temperature and soil requirements
FAO – Disasters cost global agriculture $3.26 trillion over three decades ($99B per year)
Heliyon 2023 – Farmers response to climate variability and change in rainfed farming systems: Insight from lived experiences of farmers (73.6% figure)
Heliyon 2021 – Investigating false start of the main growing season: A case of Uganda in East Africa (53% figure)
